1.title: Debugging Applications and Rollouts
1.text: Welcome to Module 11: Debugging Applications and Rollouts. This module is in the Cloud Native Application Delivery domain, and it covers the topic called Debugging. By the end you will be able to do four things. Diagnose a stuck rollout with rollout status, history and undo. Spot probe, image, Config Map and Secret mistakes. Use port forward, exec, previous logs and ephemeral containers. And separate an application fault from a platform fault, in Helm and Git Ops too.

1.title: Case Check-In: A Harbor Books Release Sticks
1.text: At Harbor Books, a new storefront release stalls. The old Pods are still there, and some new Pods never become Ready. Customers still see the old version, and the team must choose: fix forward, or roll back. The same release also goes through Helm and a Git Ops agent, so the failure may show up in either tool. In this module you find out why, and who owns the fix.

1.title: Stuck and Failed Rollouts
1.text: A rollout can stall for several reasons: quota, readiness probe failures, image pull errors, permissions, limit ranges, or application misconfiguration. The progress deadline seconds field is how long the controller waits before it reports no progress. It defaults to six hundred seconds. After that, the Deployment reports Progress Deadline Exceeded. Kubernetes only reports this. It does not roll back for you. Three commands help. Rollout status watches, rollout history lists revisions, and rollout undo goes back. Exam tip: status to see it, history to choose, undo to go back.

1.title: Probes That Misbehave
1.text: Probes cause many stuck releases. A liveness probe that is too strict restarts healthy containers, and under load that can cause cascading failures. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Endpoint Slices, so Services send it no traffic, and a rollout cannot finish. A missing startup probe for a slow starter lets the liveness probe kill the container before it is up. Liveness does not wait for readiness, so use initial delay seconds or a startup probe. Exam tip: readiness controls traffic, and liveness controls restarts.

1.title: Image, ConfigMap and Secret Errors
1.text: Four symptoms to match to causes. Image Pull Back Off usually means a wrong image name or tag, or a private registry with no image pull secret, so fix the reference or add the secret. Crash Loop Back Off means an application error, or a configuration error such as a wrong environment variable or a missing file. Read the previous logs, then the settings. An event about a Secret means the referenced Secret does not exist. The kube let keeps retrying, so create it before the Pods that need it. And an empty value means an optional Config Map or key is missing. Exam tip: read the Pod's events first.

1.title: Looking Inside a Running Application
1.text: Four commands let you look inside. Kube control logs with the previous option shows the last output of the crashed container. Exec opens a shell in a container, if the image has a shell. Port forward connects a local port to a port in a Pod, so you can test the application directly. And kube control debug adds an ephemeral container to a running Pod, which helps when the image has no shell. The snippet shows all four against the orders Pod. Exam tip: exec needs a shell in the image, and debug brings its own.

1.title: Resource Problems: OOMKilled and Throttling
1.text: Limits fail in two different ways. Over its memory limit, a container may be killed, with the reason O O M Killed, and then restarted. A C P U limit is enforced by throttling. The container is slowed down, but it is not killed. So a throttled container is slow, while an O O M killed container restarts. The diagram shows the two columns. To investigate, check kube control top and the limits, and then raise them, or fix the application. Exam tip: over the memory limit, killed. Over the C P U limit, slowed.

1.title: Helm and GitOps Failures
1.text: Release tools add their own failure states. With Helm, when you use the wait option, a release is marked failed if its Pods are not ready within the timeout, which is five minutes by default. Helm history shows it, and helm rollback returns to an earlier revision. With Git Ops, two questions are separate. Out Of Sync means the cluster differs from Git. Degraded means resources are failing, for example a crash loop. An application can be Synced and Degraded. It can also be Out Of Sync after a webhook changed an object. Exam tip: Out Of Sync is about Git, and Degraded is about the workload.

1.title: Application Fault or Platform Fault?
1.text: The last skill is deciding who owns the fix. Ask first: did the container start? If not, look at the platform: scheduling, image pull, volumes, quota, permissions and the node. Events point to these. If it started and then failed, look at the application: the logs, the configuration, the probes and the memory. Logs point to these. A failed Helm or Git Ops release is usually one of these two, seen through a tool. Exam tip: events for the platform, logs for the application.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: To recap. For rollouts, use status, history and undo, and remember that the progress deadline only reports a stall. For probes, readiness controls traffic, liveness controls restarts, and startup protects slow starters. For errors, look for a wrong image, bad settings or a missing Secret, and read the events and the previous logs. For tools, use exec, port forward, and ephemeral containers through kube control debug. For limits, memory over the limit is O O M Killed, and C P U over the limit is throttled. And for delivery tools, Helm marks a release failed after the timeout, and Git Ops separates Out Of Sync from Degraded. Now seven practice questions.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A rollout is stuck, and the progress deadline has passed. What does Kubernetes do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. After the deadline the Progressing condition becomes False, with the reason Progress Deadline Exceeded. Kubernetes does not roll back by itself, although a higher-level tool can act on the condition.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. The new Harbor Books storefront release is stuck, and the team wants to return to the previous version quickly. Which command does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The undo command returns the Deployment to its previous revision. Status and history only show information, and deleting the Deployment removes the application instead of restoring it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. New Pods of a Deployment keep failing their readiness probe, although their logs show no errors. What is the effect? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the Endpoint Slices of its Services, so it gets no traffic and does not count as ready for the rollout. Restarts come from failing liveness probes.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. A Harbor Books Pod stays in an error state, and its events say that the Secret it references does not exist. What should the team do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. The kube let keeps retrying a Pod whose Secret cannot be fetched, and reports an event, so creating the Secret fixes it. Memory limits, probes and nodes are unrelated to a missing Secret.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. The image of a Pod has no shell, so kube control exec cannot open one. Which command lets the team troubleshoot inside that Pod? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The debug command adds an ephemeral container with its own image and shell to a running Pod. Port forwarding tests connectivity, undo changes the revision, and top shows resource use.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A Harbor Books container is restarted again and again, and its last state shows the reason O O M Killed. What does that tell the team? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. O O M Killed means that the container used more memory than its limit allowed, so the team should look for a leak or raise the limit. A C P U limit slows a container down but does not kill it, an image problem shows as Image Pull Back Off, and node pressure eviction ends the Pod instead of restarting a container.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A Git Ops tool shows an application as Synced but Degraded. What does that tell you? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Sync status asks whether the cluster matches Git, and health asks whether the resources work. Synced with Degraded means the manifests were applied, but a workload, such as a crash-looping Pod, is unhealthy.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, B: it reports Progress Deadline Exceeded, and does nothing else. Question two, D: rollout undo goes back to the previous revision. Question three, A: a failing readiness probe removes the Pod from the endpoints. Question four, C: create the missing Secret, and the kube let retries. Question five, B: kube control debug adds an ephemeral container. Question six, D: O O M Killed means the container exceeded its memory limit. Question seven, A: Synced matches Git, and Degraded means failing resources.
